v1213: David, 45, a school administrator in Chennai, who grew up in a troubled home
v1214: David's body never seemed to relax. He startled at sudden noises, sat with his back to the wall in restaurants and could not sleep without the lights on. He had headaches and stomach problems. When his wife touched his shoulder from behind, he jumped. He thought this was just his personality. At church he heard a talk about trauma and the body and realised his symptoms matched. As a child, David lived with a father who drank and often became violent at night. He learned to listen for footsteps, to be ready to hide or protect his mother. Now, decades later, his body still behaved as if danger was near.
v1215: Research suggests that childhood trauma can leave the nervous system stuck on high alert. The brain's alarm centre becomes very sensitive, and the body stays ready for danger. This is called hypervigilance. Even when life is safe, small triggers like footsteps, raised voices or darkness can send the body back to old memories. David's younger self still felt unsafe and was trying to protect him. His stress response, with cortisol and adrenaline, never fully switched off. Without help, the body does not know the danger is over. Felt safety, meaning the body truly feels safe and not just knows it, is needed for healing.
v1216: In counselling, David read Psalm 91:1, about dwelling under the shadow of the Almighty. He began to imagine God as a safe Father who would never harm him. Slowly he let his younger self rest in God's care.

v1222: The gospel offers David a Father who is safe. "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty" (Psalm 91:1). Jesus understands suffering and fear (Hebrews 4:15). David also experienced healing through others. His counsellor, his wife and a men's prayer group offered safe relationships where he could share his story. "He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds" (Psalm 147:3). God's love reached the frightened boy inside the grown man.
v1223: God designed the brain to protect us from danger, but also to return to calm when danger passes. Research suggests that trauma interrupts this process. Healing comes through repeated experiences of safety, in the body as well as the mind. Safe relationships, gentle routines, grounding and calming practices help widen the window of tolerance, so that triggers no longer overwhelm. Imagining God's protective presence can bring a deep sense of felt safety. God made our brains changeable, so even long-held patterns can heal over time.
